paragraphs: A curved-brim fitted cap built at 16,068 polygons, which is the range where a hat still reads as fabric in a close-up but costs almost nothing when you put it on a stadium crowd. The shape carries the parts people actually look at: the panel seams, the eyelets, the button at the crown and the slight lift where the brim leaves the band. Nine texture maps do the rest, so the stitching and the weave come from the material rather than from geometry you would pay for twice.

This page holds the whole run of caps built on that shape. Alongside the plain version there are NASCAR team caps, a New Era classic curved visor, a vintage 00s racing hat and a flame-stripe brim. Same mesh underneath, different livery on top, which is why they sit together instead of scattering across five near-identical pages. The branded ones carry editorial terms; the plain cap does not, and that is usually the one that ends up in commercial work.

It has sold 439 times, mostly into advertising and game work, where a cap is set dressing that still has to survive being looked at. CheckMate Pro certification means the scene opens clean: real-world scale, no stray geometry, materials named the way a lighting artist expects to find them.

The Model 3 exterior at 116,225 polygons and 130,476 vertices, modelled to the proportions that make this car recognisable from fifty metres: the low nose with no grille, the single unbroken roof glass, the flush door handles. Nine texture maps cover the body, the glass and the wheels. It is a driving-shot car, built to be seen in motion or parked in an architectural scene rather than opened up and inspected panel by panel.

Two further versions sit on this page. The rigged one turns the wheels and the steering, which is what a walk-around or a street loop needs. The simple-interior one gives you a cabin that holds up through the window glass without loading a full trim set nobody sees from outside. Pick by shot, not by completeness.

Licensing is editorial only. Tesla owns the marks and the car design, so this model belongs in news, commentary, education and film, not in advertising for a product and not where it might imply endorsement. That restriction comes from the manufacturer and applies to any faithful model of a current production car. If a project needs commercial clearance, a generic electric sedan is the honest answer, and we build those too.

A single phalaenopsis stem at 2,358 polygons, all quads, which is about as light as a believable flower gets. The petals are modelled rather than cut out of an alpha map, so the shape survives being lit from behind and does not go flat when the camera moves around it. Five texture maps carry the vein pattern and the colour fall from throat to petal edge.

That weight is the point. An orchid is a dressing prop: it goes on the reception desk, the hotel nightstand, the corner of a kitchen counter. You place twenty of them in a scene and never think about them again. At two thousand polygons each, twenty cost less than one hero plant, and the silhouette still reads at the size it appears on screen.

StemCell certification means the asset is built to a shared standard for runtime engines, so it drops into Unreal or Unity without a rebuild. It has sold 326 times, largely into architectural visualisation, where the difference between an empty room and a lived-in one is usually three plants and a bowl of fruit.

A 20-foot ISO shipping container at 42,248 polygons, built to the real specification: corrugation pitch, corner castings, the cam-lock door gear and the lashing points that everything else in a port scene hangs from. Five texture maps carry the paint, the weld lines and the wear. Because the outer dimensions are the standard ones, it stacks and lines up with itself without anyone nudging numbers.

Eight versions share this page. Green, blue, brown and white are the same box in different liveries, and there is a Linde reach stacker carrying one, rigged, for when the container has to be lifted rather than parked. That combination is why the page exists: a port is never one container, it is forty of them in four colours and a machine moving one.

It has sold 308 times, into logistics visualisation, architecture and simulation. CheckMate Pro certification means real-world scale, so it sits correctly next to a truck chassis or a crane without being measured first.

The 2020 Transit cargo van at 153,391 polygons and 174,527 vertices, with seventeen texture maps across the body, the glass, the lamps and the wheels. The density goes where a van is actually looked at: the front end, the sliding door track, the rear door seams and the ribbing along the load side. This is the working configuration, panel van with no side glass, which is what most commercial scenes need.
A rigged version and a white variant sit alongside it. The rigged one steers and rolls, which matters because a delivery van is almost always moving in the shot or being loaded in it.

Sold 289 times, mostly into simulation, advertising and architectural work, where a parked van does the job of telling you the building is in use. Licensing is editorial only: Ford owns the marks and the body design, so this model belongs in editorial, educational and film contexts rather than in advertising for a product. That limit is set by the manufacturer and applies to any faithful model of a current vehicle.
